results.title: $G$-permutable subgroups
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A subgroup $A$ of a group $G$ is $G$-permutable when for every subgroup $B$ of $G$ there is $x \in G$ such that $A B^x = B^x A$, where $B^x = x B x^{-1}$ is the conjugate of $B$ by $x$ and the products are products of subsets of $G$.

results.title: Permutable subgroups of large alternating groups are trivial or the whole group
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: There is a natural number $n$ such that for every $m > n$, every $A_m$-permutable subgroup of the alternating group $A_m$ is either the trivial subgroup or $A_m$ itself. Here a subgroup $A$ of a group $G$ is $G$-permutable when for every subgroup $B$ of $G$ there is $x \in G$ with $A B^x = B^x A$, where $B^x = x B x^{-1}$.

results.title: Absolute values in positive characteristic are nonarchimedean
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $p > 0$. Then every real-valued absolute value $v$ on $K$ is nonarchimedean: $v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for all $x, y \in K$.

results.title: Absolute values on finite fields are trivial
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a finite field and $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $K$. Then $v(x) = 1$ for every nonzero $x \in K$.

results.title: Topology induced by an absolute value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $K$. The topology induced by $v$ on $K$ is the topology pulled back along the identity map from $K$ to $K$ equipped with the norm $v$; equivalently, it is the metric topology of the distance $d(x, y) = v(x - y)$ on $K$.

results.title: Absolute values inducing the same topology are equivalent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field and $v$, $w$ real-valued absolute values on $K$. The topologies induced on $K$ by $v$ and by $w$ are equal if and only if $v$ and $w$ are equivalent.

results.title: Nonarchimedean criterion for absolute values
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $K$. Then $v$ is nonarchimedean, that is, $v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for all $x, y \in K$, if and only if $v(n) \le 1$ for every natural number $n$, viewed as the element $n \cdot 1$ of $K$.

results.title: Absolute values bounded by one on the natural numbers are nonarchimedean
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $K$. If $v(n) \le 1$ for every natural number $n$, viewed as the element $n \cdot 1$ of $K$, then $v$ is nonarchimedean: $v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for all $x, y \in K$.

results.title: Nonarchimedean criterion using positive integers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a field and $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $K$. Then $v$ is nonarchimedean, that is, $v(x + y) \le \max(v(x), v(y))$ for all $x, y \in K$, if and only if $v(n) \le 1$ for every positive integer $n$, viewed as the element $n \cdot 1$ of $K$.

results.title: Powers of an absolute value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring, $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $R$ and $c$ a real number with $0 < c \le 1$. The $c$-th power of $v$ is the real-valued absolute value $x \mapsto v(x)^c$ on $R$.

results.title: Values of a power of an absolute value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a semiring, $v$ a real-valued absolute value on $R$ and $c$ a real number with $0 < c \le 1$. The $c$-th power of $v$ takes the value $v(x)^c$ at every $x \in R$.

results.title: Equichordal point
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $K$ be a subset of the Euclidean plane. A point $P$ is an equichordal point of $K$ if $P$ lies in the interior of $K$ and there is a real $L > 0$ such that for every unit vector $u$ there are reals $a > 0$ and $b > 0$ for which $P + a u$ and $P - b u$ lie in the boundary (frontier) of $K$, the open segment between $P - b u$ and $P + a u$ lies in the interior of $K$, and the distance between $P + a u$ and…

results.title: Equichordal point theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $K$ be a compact convex subset of the Euclidean plane with nonempty interior. Then $K$ does not have two distinct equichordal points: there are no points $P \ne Q$ of the plane such that both $P$ and $Q$ are equichordal points of $K$.

results.title: Positive definite functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is positive definite when for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all $t_1, \dots, t_n \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $z_1, \dots, z_n \in \mathbb{C}$, the sum $S = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \varphi(t_i - t_j) \, z_i \, \overline{z_j}$ is real and nonnegative, that is, $\operatorname{Im} S = 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} S \ge 0$.

results.title: Positive definite real-valued functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is positive definite when its composition with the inclusion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is positive definite, that is, when for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all $t_1, \dots, t_n \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $z_1, \dots, z_n \in \mathbb{C}$, the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \varphi(t_i - t_j) \, z_i \, \overline{z_j}$ is a nonnegative real number.

results.title: Characteristic functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is a characteristic function when there is a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ whose characteristic function equals $\varphi$, that is, $\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{itx} \, d\mu(x) = \varphi(t)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

results.title: Real-valued characteristic functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A function $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is a real-valued characteristic function when its composition with the inclusion $\mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is a characteristic function, that is, when there is a probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $\int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{itx} \, d\mu(x) = \varphi(t)$ for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

results.title: Forward direction of Bochner's theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\varphi : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ be the characteristic function of a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$. Then $\varphi$ is continuous, positive definite, and satisfies $\varphi(0) = 1$.

results.title: Characteristic functions are positive definite
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ with characteristic function $\varphi_\mu(t) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} e^{itx} \, d\mu(x)$. Then $\varphi_\mu$ is positive definite: for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, all $t_1, \dots, t_n \in \mathbb{R}$ and all $z_1, \dots, z_n \in \mathbb{C}$, the sum $\sum_{i=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \varphi_\mu(t_i - t_j) \, z_i \, \overline{z_j}$ is a nonnegative real number.

results.title: Continuous mapping theorem for weak convergence of probability measures
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mu_n$ ($n \in \mathbb{N}$) and $\mu$ be probability measures on $\mathbb{R}$, and let $g : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a measurable function whose set of discontinuity points has $\mu$-measure zero. If $\mu_n$ converges weakly to $\mu$ as $n \to \infty$, then the pushforward probability measures $\mu_n \circ g^{-1}$ converge weakly to $\mu \circ g^{-1}$.

results.title: Next term of a greedy $B_h$-set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $h$ and $a$ be natural numbers and $A$ a set of natural numbers. Then $a$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $A$ if $a$ is greater than every element of $A$, the set $A \cup \{a\}$ is a $B_h$-set, and for every natural number $b < a$ that is greater than every element of $A$, the set $A \cup \{b\}$ is not a $B_h$-set.

results.title: Fourth positive term of the greedy $B_h$-set
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $h$ and $a$, we say that $a$ is the fourth positive element $a_4(h)$ of the greedy $B_h$-set if $1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0\}$, $h + 1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1\}$, $h^2 + h + 1$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1, h + 1\}$, and $a$ is the next greedy $B_h$ choice after $\{0, 1, h + 1, h^2 + h + 1\}$.

results.title: Instances of MINIMUM BISECTION
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: An instance of MINIMUM BISECTION is a triple $(n, es, K)$ of a natural number $n$ (the number of vertices), a list $es$ of pairs of natural numbers (the edge list) and a natural number $K$ (the bound on the number of crossing edges).

results.title: Well-formed MINIMUM BISECTION instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, es, K)$ of MINIMUM BISECTION is well formed when $n$ is even, the list $es$ has no repeated entries, and every entry $(u, v)$ of $es$ satisfies $u < n$, $v < n$ and $u \ne v$, and $(v, u)$ is not an entry of $es$.

results.title: Feasible MINIMUM BISECTION instances
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An instance $(n, es, K)$ of MINIMUM BISECTION is feasible when there is a set $S \subseteq \{0, \dots, n - 1\}$ with $\lfloor n / 2 \rfloor$ elements such that no sublist of $es$ (a list obtained from $es$ by deleting entries) with $K + 1$ entries consists only of entries $(u, v)$ with exactly one of $u$ and $v$ in $S$; that is, at most $K$ entries of $es$ have exactly one endpoint in $S$.

results.title: The decision problem MINIMUM BISECTION
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The decision problem MINIMUM BISECTION accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of instances, to an instance $(n, es, K)$ of MINIMUM BISECTION that is well formed and feasible (its vertices split into two sets of $n / 2$ vertices with at most $K$ entries of $es$ between them). Bitstrings that do not decode are rejected.

results.title: MINIMUM BISECTION is NP-complete
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The decision problem MINIMUM BISECTION belongs to NP, and every decision problem in NP reduces to it by a polynomial-time many-one reduction.

results.title: Number of keys of the empty tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The empty binary tree has $0$ nodes.

results.title: Number of keys of a node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of nodes of a binary tree $t$. For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, the node with key $k$, left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$ has $|l| + |r| + 1$ nodes.

results.title: Weight of a binary tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Nievergelt–Reingold weight $w(t)$ of a binary tree $t$ is its number of keys plus one. Equivalently, it counts the external leaves: the empty tree has weight $1$, and the weight of a node is the sum of the weights of its two children.

results.title: Weight-balanced trees
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a binary tree $t$ and $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight. A binary tree is weight-balanced, or satisfies the invariant $\mathrm{BB}[1/4]$, when it is empty, or when it is a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ such that $L$ and $R$ are weight-balanced, $4\,w(L) \le 3(w(L) + w(R))$ and $4\,w(R) \le 3(w(L) + w(R))$. Since the weight of a node is $w(L) + w(R)$, this says…

results.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For binary trees $L$, $R$ and a key $k$, write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$, $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight, $w = w(L) + w(R)$, and $\langle X, x, Y \rangle$ for the node with key $x$, left subtree $X$ and right subtree $Y$. The rebalanced node $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ is defined as follows. If $3w < 4\,w(L)$, then $L = \langle A, a, B \rangle$ is a node; if $|B| \le 2|A|$, the result is the…

results.title: Weight-balanced insertion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, the insertion $\mathrm{insert}(x, t)$ of $x$ into a binary tree $t$ is defined by recursion on $t$. Into the empty tree it gives the single node with key $x$. Into the node $N$ with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ it gives $\mathrm{balance}(\mathrm{insert}(x, L), k, R)$ if $x < k$, $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, \mathrm{insert}(x, R))$ if $k < x$, and $N$ itself if…

results.title: Weight-balanced tree from a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The tree built from a list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ of elements of a linearly ordered type is obtained from the empty tree by inserting $x_n, x_{n-1}, \dots, x_1$ in this order with weight-balanced insertion; the empty list gives the empty tree.

results.title: Building a weight-balanced node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be weight-balanced trees and $k$ a key, and write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$. If $4(|L| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2)$ and $4(|R| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2)$, then the node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is weight-balanced.

results.title: Weight form of the balance condition at a node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$ and $w(t) = |t| + 1$ for its weight. Let $N$ be the node with key $k$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$. Then $N$ is weight-balanced if and only if $L$ and $R$ are weight-balanced, $4\,w(L) \le 3\,w(N)$ and $4\,w(R) \le 3\,w(N)$. This is the classical $\mathrm{BB}[1/4]$ invariant: each child has weight at most three quarters of the weight of the node.

results.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing preserves the number of keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of nodes of a binary tree $t$. For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, the weight-balanced rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ has exactly $|l| + |r| + 1$ nodes.

results.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing restores balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ and $R$ be weight-balanced trees and $k$ a key, and write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a tree $t$. If $4(|L| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2) + 1$ and $4(|R| + 1) \le 3(|L| + |R| + 2) + 1$, then the rebalanced node $\mathrm{balance}(L, k, R)$ is weight-balanced.

results.title: Membership after weight-balanced rebalancing
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For binary trees $l$ and $r$ and a key $k$, an element $x$ occurs in the weight-balanced rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ exactly when $x$ occurs in $l$, $x = k$, or $x$ occurs in $r$. Membership is structural: $x$ is the key of some node.

results.title: Weight-balanced rebalancing preserves ordering
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order, let $l$ and $r$ be ordered binary trees (strict binary search trees), and let $k$ be a key such that every key of $l$ is less than $k$ and every key of $r$ is greater than $k$. Then the weight-balanced rebalancing of $l$, $k$, $r$ is ordered.

results.title: Weight-balanced insertion adds at most one key
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$, the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of $x$ has at most one more node than $t$.

results.title: Weight-balanced insertion does not decrease the number of keys
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every key $x$ and every binary tree $t$, the number of nodes of $t$ is at most the number of nodes of the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of $x$.

results.title: Weight-balanced insertion preserves balance
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and every weight-balanced tree $t$, the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ with weight-balanced insertion is weight-balanced.

results.title: Membership after weight-balanced insertion
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For all keys $x$, $y$ and every binary tree $t$, $y$ occurs in the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of $x$ exactly when $y = x$ or $y$ occurs in $t$.

results.title: Weight-balanced insertion preserves the search-tree order
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys be linearly ordered. If a binary tree $t$ is ordered as a search tree (at every node, every key of the left subtree is strictly smaller and every key of the right subtree strictly larger than the key at the node), then the tree obtained from $t$ by weight-balanced insertion of any key $x$ is again ordered.

results.title: Weight-balanced trees built by insertion are balanced
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $x_1, \dots, x_n$ of elements of a linearly ordered type, the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting $x_n, x_{n-1}, \dots, x_1$ in this order with weight-balanced insertion is weight-balanced.

results.title: Weight-balanced trees built from a list are ordered
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every list $xs$, the weight-balanced tree built from $xs$ by repeated insertion is ordered, that is, a strict binary search tree.

results.title: Membership in a weight-balanced tree built from a list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let the keys carry a linear order. For every key $x$ and every list $xs$, $x$ occurs in the weight-balanced tree built from $xs$ by repeated insertion exactly when $x$ is an element of $xs$.

results.title: Exponential weight lower bound for weight-balanced trees
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $w(t)$ for the weight of a binary tree $t$ (its number of keys plus one), and measure height so that the empty tree has height $0$ and a node has height one more than the taller of its children. If $t$ is weight balanced with parameter $1/4$ (at every node, each child has weight at most three quarters of the weight of the node) and has height $k + 1$ for a natural number $k$, then $w(t) \ge (4/3)^k$; in…

results.title: Height of a weight-balanced tree is logarithmic
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $|t|$ for the number of keys of a binary tree $t$ and $h(t)$ for its height, where the empty tree has height $0$ and a node has height one more than the larger height of its two subtrees. If $t$ is weight-balanced, then $h(t) \le \lfloor \log_2 ((|t| + 1)^3) \rfloor + 1$.

outside: A predicate holding at every key of a binary tree
A predicate holds at all keys of a binary tree iff it holds at all its members

results.title: Pairwise model on a tree
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: For a type $\alpha$ of values and $n \in \mathbb{N}$, a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ consists of a parent $p(k + 1) \in \{0, \dots, k\}$ for each vertex $k + 1$ with $k < n$ (so vertex $0$ is the root and every vertex comes after its parent), a unary factor $\varphi_i : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ for each vertex $i \le n$, and for each $k < n$ a pairwise factor $\psi_k(a, b) \in \mathbb{R}$ on the…

results.title: Parent of a vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$, for $k < n$ the parent of vertex $k + 1$ is the parent recorded by the model, an element of $\{0, \dots, k\}$, regarded as one of the vertices $0, \dots, n$.

results.title: Weight of an assignment in a tree model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type and let $m$ be a pairwise model on a tree with vertices $0, \dots, n$, with unary factors $\varphi_i : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ for each vertex $i$, and with factor $\psi_k : \alpha \times \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ on the edge between vertex $k + 1$ and its parent $p(k + 1)$ for each $k < n$. The unnormalized weight of an assignment $x : \{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$ is the real number

results.title: Parent of the last vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: In a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, this is the parent of the last vertex $n + 1$, regarded as one of the vertices $0, \dots, n$ of the tree with the last vertex removed.

results.title: Message from the last vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and consider a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with unary factors $\varphi_i$ and pairwise factors $\psi_k$. The message from the last vertex $n + 1$ to its parent is the function $\mu : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ given by $\mu(a) = \sum_{b \in \alpha} \psi_n(b, a) \, \varphi_{n+1}(b)$, where $\psi_n$ is the factor of the edge between vertex $n + 1$ and its parent.

results.title: Eliminating the last vertex of a tree model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite, let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with parents $p$, unary factors $\varphi_i$ and pairwise factors $\psi_k$, and let $\mu$ be the message from the last vertex $n + 1$ to its parent $q = p(n + 1)$. Eliminating the last vertex gives the pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ in which vertex $k + 1$ has parent $p(k + 1)$ and edge factor $\psi_k$ for…

results.title: One step of variable elimination
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite, let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with weight $w$, and let $m'$ be the model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ obtained from $m$ by eliminating the last vertex, with weight $w'$. Then for every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ we have $\sum_x w(x) \, g(x_0) = \sum_y w'(y) \, g(y_0)$, where $x$ ranges over all assignments $\{0, \dots, n + 1\} \to \alpha$ and…

results.title: Root message of a tree model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite. The root message of a pairwise tree model $m$ on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ is the function $r_m : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by recursion on $n$: if $n = 0$, it is the unary factor of the root $0$; if $m$ is a model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, it is $r_{m'}$, where $m'$ is the model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ obtained from $m$ by eliminating the last vertex.

results.title: Variable elimination is exact
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message $r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then for every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ of the root value, $\sum_x w(x) \, g(x_0) = \sum_{a \in \alpha} r(a) \, g(a)$, where $x$ ranges over all assignments $\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$.

results.title: Variable elimination computes the partition function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message $r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then the partition function of $m$ is the total root message: $\sum_x w(x) = \sum_{a \in \alpha} r(a)$, where $x$ ranges over all assignments $\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$.

results.title: Variable elimination computes the unnormalized root marginal
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be finite and let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with weight $w$ and root message $r : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$. Then for every $a \in \alpha$ the unnormalized marginal of the root at $a$ equals $r(a)$, that is, $\sum_x w(x) = r(a)$, where $x$ ranges over the assignments $\{0, \dots, n\} \to \alpha$ with $x_0 = a$.

results.title: Removing the last vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, the tree model on $0, \dots, n$ with the same parents, unary factors and edge factors: the last vertex, which is a leaf, is removed together with its unary factor and the factor of its edge.

results.title: Summing out the last vertex preserves weighted sums at the other vertices
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ with values in a finite type $\alpha$, and let $m'$ be the model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ obtained from $m$ by summing out its last vertex. Write $w_m$ and $w_{m'}$ for their unnormalized weights. Then for every vertex $v \le n$ and every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$,

results.title: Sum-product belief
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The belief of each vertex of a tree model over a finite set of values, computed by sum-product message passing: the product of its unary factor, the messages from its subtree and the message from its parent. Recursively, in a model with a single vertex the belief of that vertex is its unary factor; in a model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ the belief of the last vertex at a value $b$ is its unary factor at $b$…

results.title: Downward message to the last vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ over a finite set of values, the message from the parent $p$ of the last vertex to the last vertex at a value $b$ is the sum over all values $a$ of $\psi(b, a)\, \beta(a)$, where $\psi$ is the factor of the edge between the last vertex and $p$ (last vertex first) and $\beta(a)$ is the belief of $p$ at $a$ in the model without the last vertex.

results.title: Belief propagation is exact on trees
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model on the vertices $0, \dots, n$ with values in a finite type $\alpha$, let $w$ be its unnormalized weight, and let $b_v$ be the belief of vertex $v$ computed by sum-product message passing. Then for every vertex $v$ and every function $g : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$,

results.title: Beliefs are the unnormalized marginals
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every tree model over a finite set of values, every vertex $v$ and every value $a$, the belief of $v$ at $a$ is the unnormalized marginal of $v$ at $a$: the sum of the weights of all assignments $x$ with $x_v = a$.

results.title: Belief at the root is the root message
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every tree model over a finite set of values, the belief of the root, vertex $0$, is the root message computed by variable elimination: the two agree at every value.

results.title: Nonnegative factors
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A tree model has nonnegative factors when all its unary factors and all its edge factors take only nonnegative values.

results.title: Max-product message
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ over a finite nonempty set of values, the max-product message from the last vertex to its parent at a value $a$ is the maximum over all values $b$ of $\psi(b, a)\, \phi(b)$, where $\psi$ is the factor of the edge between the last vertex and its parent and $\phi$ is the unary factor of the last vertex.

results.title: Maximizing out the last vertex
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree model with vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$ over a finite nonempty set of values, the tree model on $0, \dots, n$ with the same parents and edge factors whose unary factor at the parent of the last vertex is multiplied by the max-product message of the last vertex; the other unary factors are unchanged.

results.title: Max-product value
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a tree model over a finite nonempty set of values, the value computed by maximizing out the vertices from the last one down: for a single vertex it is the maximum of its unary factor over all values, and for more vertices it is the max-product value of the model with the last vertex maximized out.

results.title: Max-product decoding
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An assignment of a tree model over a finite nonempty set of values, defined by recursion on the number of vertices. For a single vertex, its value is one that maximizes its unary factor. For vertices $0, \dots, n + 1$, the vertices $0, \dots, n$ get the decoding of the model with the last vertex maximized out, and the last vertex gets a value $b$ maximizing $\psi(b, a)\, \phi(b)$, where $a$ is the decoded value of…

results.title: The max-product value bounds every weight
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model with values in a finite nonempty type $\alpha$ whose unary and pairwise factors are all nonnegative, and let $M$ be its max-product value, obtained by maximizing out the vertices from the last one down. Then every assignment of values in $\alpha$ to the vertices has weight at most $M$.

results.title: Max-product decoding attains the max-product value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model with values in a finite nonempty type, and let $M$ be its max-product value, obtained by maximizing out the vertices from the last one down. Then the weight of the assignment produced by max-product decoding equals $M$.

results.title: Max-product decoding finds a MAP assignment
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $m$ be a pairwise tree model with values in a finite nonempty type $\alpha$ whose unary and pairwise factors are all nonnegative. Then every assignment of values in $\alpha$ to the vertices has weight at most the weight of the assignment produced by max-product decoding.

results.title: Pricing scan
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given rational residual weights $r$ on the vertices, a rational total price $P$ and a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices), the pricing scan processes the edges in order: an edge $(u, v)$ has price $\delta = \min(r(u), r(v))$, which is subtracted from the residual weight of $u$ and of $v$ (once if $u = v$) and added to the total price. The result is the final pair of residual weights and total price, and the…

results.title: Pricing method for weighted vertex cover
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given rational weights $w$ on a finite vertex set $V$ and a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices), run the pricing scan on the list starting from residual weights $w$ and total price $0$, then return the set of vertices whose final residual weight is $0$. On top of the cost of the scan, the selection costs $|V|$ time units.

results.title: Pricing scan: residual weights stay between $0$ and their start
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be rational residual weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $P$ be a rational number and let $L$ be a list of edges. If the pricing scan of $L$ from residual weights $r$ and total price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$, then $0 \le r'(v) \le r(v)$ for every vertex $v$.

results.title: Pricing scan: every edge has an exhausted endpoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $r$ be rational residual weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $P$ be a rational number and let $L$ be a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices). If the pricing scan of $L$ from residual weights $r$ and total price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$, then every pair $(u, v)$ in $L$ has $r'(u) = 0$ or $r'(v) = 0$.

results.title: Pricing scan: the vertices pay at most twice the price
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $V$ be a finite vertex set, let $r$ be rational residual weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $P$ be a rational number and let $L$ be a list of edges. If the pricing scan of $L$ from residual weights $r$ and total price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$ and total price $P'$, then $\sum_{v \in V} (r(v) - r'(v)) \le 2 (P' - P)$.

results.title: Pricing scan: the total price is at most what a cover pays
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C$ be a finite set of vertices, let $r$ be rational residual weights with $r(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $P$ be a rational number, and let $L$ be a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices) such that every pair $(u, v)$ in $L$ has $u \in C$ or $v \in C$. If the pricing scan of $L$ from residual weights $r$ and total price $P$ ends with residual weights $r'$ and total price $P'$, then…

results.title: The pricing method covers every listed edge
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be rational weights on a finite vertex set with $w(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, and let $L$ be a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices). For every pair $(u, v)$ in $L$, $u$ or $v$ belongs to the set returned by the pricing method on $w$ and $L$.

results.title: The pricing method returns a vertex cover
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set, let $w$ be rational vertex weights with $w(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, and let $L$ be a list of ordered pairs of vertices such that for every edge $uv$ of $G$, the pair $(u, v)$ or the pair $(v, u)$ is in $L$. Then the set returned by the pricing method on $w$ and $L$ is a vertex cover of $G$.

results.title: The pricing method weighs at most twice any cover of the listed edges
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $w$ be rational weights on a finite vertex set with $w(v) \ge 0$ for every vertex $v$, let $L$ be a list of edges (ordered pairs of vertices), and let $C$ be a set of vertices such that every pair $(u, v)$ in $L$ has $u \in C$ or $v \in C$. Then the total weight of the set returned by the pricing method on $w$ and $L$ is at most $2 \sum_{v \in C} w(v)$.

results.title: Running time of the pricing method
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all rational vertex weights $w$ on a finite vertex set $V$ and every list $L$ of edges, the pricing method on $w$ and $L$ takes exactly $|L| + |V|$ time units, where $|L|$ is the length of the list: one unit per listed edge and one per vertex.

results.title: Real amplitude vectors
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a type $\alpha$ (the search space), a real amplitude vector indexed by $\alpha$ is a function $\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, assigning a real amplitude to each point of $\alpha$.

results.title: Phase oracle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a type $\alpha$ and a finite set $M \subseteq \alpha$ of marked elements, the phase oracle sends a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on $\alpha$ to the amplitude vector whose value at $x$ is $-\psi(x)$ if $x \in M$ and $\psi(x)$ if $x \notin M$; that is, it negates exactly the amplitudes at the marked elements.

results.title: Squared norm of an amplitude vector
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite type $\alpha$ and a real amplitude vector $\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, the squared norm of $\psi$ is its squared Euclidean norm $\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi(x)^2$.

results.title: Probability of the marked outcomes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on a type $\alpha$ and a finite set $M \subseteq \alpha$ of marked elements, the marked probability is $\sum_{x \in M} \psi(x)^2$. When $\alpha$ is finite and $\psi$ has squared norm $1$, this is the probability of observing a marked outcome.

results.title: Uniform amplitude vector
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite type $\alpha$, the uniform amplitude vector on $\alpha$ is the real amplitude vector whose value at every point is $1/\sqrt{|\alpha|}$, where $|\alpha|$ is the number of elements of $\alpha$.

results.title: The uniform amplitude vector is normalized
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every nonempty finite type $\alpha$, the uniform amplitude vector on $\alpha$ has squared Euclidean norm $1$.

results.title: Mean amplitude
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite type $\alpha$ and a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on $\alpha$, the mean amplitude of $\psi$ is $\bigl(\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi(x)\bigr) / |\alpha|$, the arithmetic mean of its amplitudes. When $\alpha$ is empty it is $0$.

results.title: Inversion about the mean
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite type $\alpha$, the diffusion operator sends a real amplitude vector $\psi$ on $\alpha$ to the amplitude vector $x \mapsto 2\bar\psi - \psi(x)$, where $\bar\psi$ is the arithmetic mean of the amplitudes of $\psi$.

results.title: Grover step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite type and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a set of marked elements. Write $O_M$ for the phase oracle, which negates the amplitudes at the points of $M$, and $D$ for inversion about the mean, which sends an amplitude vector $\varphi$ on $\alpha$ to $x \mapsto 2\bar\varphi - \varphi(x)$, where $\bar\varphi$ is the arithmetic mean of the amplitudes of $\varphi$. One Grover step sends a real amplitude…

results.title: Symmetric amplitude vector
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a search space $\alpha$, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The symmetric amplitude vector with marked amplitude $a$ and unmarked amplitude $b$ is the real amplitude vector on $\alpha$ whose value is $a$ at every element of $M$ and $b$ at every element outside $M$.

results.title: Mean amplitude after the phase oracle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite search space of size $N$, let $M^c$ be the set of unmarked elements, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. The oracle mean is $(|M^c|\, b - |M|\, a) / N$.

results.title: Marked amplitude after a Grover step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite search space of size $N$, let $M^c$ be the set of unmarked elements, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. With $\mu = (|M^c|\, b - |M|\, a) / N$, the next marked amplitude is $2\mu + a$.

results.title: Unmarked amplitude after a Grover step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite search space of size $N$, let $M^c$ be the set of unmarked elements, and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$. With $\mu = (|M^c|\, b - |M|\, a) / N$, the next unmarked amplitude is $2\mu - b$.

results.title: Grover angle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a finite search space $\alpha$ and a marked set $M \subseteq \alpha$, the Grover angle of $M$ is $\theta = \arcsin \sqrt{|M| / |\alpha|}$, where the quotient $|M| / |\alpha|$ is taken to be $0$ when $\alpha$ is empty.

results.title: Symmetric Grover state at a given angle
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set with complement $M^c$. For a real number $\varphi$, this is the real amplitude vector on $\alpha$ whose value is $\sin\varphi / \sqrt{|M|}$ at every point of $M$ and $\cos\varphi / \sqrt{|M^c|}$ at every point of $M^c$.

results.title: Grover iterate
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$ and a real amplitude vector $\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$, the $k$-th Grover iterate of $\psi$ is the vector obtained by applying the Grover step for $M$ to $\psi$ $k$ times; the $0$-th iterate is $\psi$ itself.

results.title: Grover iteration preserves the squared norm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite search space and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set. For every real amplitude vector $\psi : \alpha \to \mathbb{R}$ and every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\psi_k$ be the vector obtained from $\psi$ by applying the Grover step for $M$ $k$ times. Then $\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi_k(x)^2 = \sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi(x)^2$.

results.title: Grover iterates of the uniform state are unit vectors
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a nonempty finite search space, $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set, and $u$ the uniform amplitude vector, given by $u(x) = 1/\sqrt{|\alpha|}$ for every $x \in \alpha$. For every $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\psi_k$ be the vector obtained from $u$ by applying the Grover step for $M$ $k$ times. Then $\sum_{x \in \alpha} \psi_k(x)^2 = 1$.

results.title: Grover phase
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space, $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set and $\theta$ the Grover angle of $M$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, the Grover phase of $M$ after $k$ iterations is the real number $(2k + 1)\theta$.

results.title: Exact success probability of Grover search
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a finite search space and $M \subseteq \alpha$ a marked set such that both $M$ and its complement are nonempty, and let $\theta = \arcsin \sqrt{|M| / |\alpha|}$ be the Grover angle of $M$. For $k \in \mathbb{N}$, let $\psi_k$ be the vector obtained by applying the Grover step for $M$ $k$ times to the uniform amplitude vector, whose value is $1/\sqrt{|\alpha|}$ at every point. Then the marked…

results.title: Standard Grover iteration count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $M$ be a set of marked elements of a finite search space of size $N$, and let $\theta = \arcsin \sqrt{|M| / N}$ be its Grover angle. The standard iteration count is $\lfloor \pi / (4\theta) \rfloor$, the largest natural number at most $\pi / (4\theta)$; it is $0$ when $\theta = 0$, that is, when no element is marked.

results.title: One Grover iteration suffices when a quarter is marked
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a nonempty set of marked elements of a finite search space of size $N$ with $4|M| = N$. Starting from the uniform amplitude vector, one Grover iteration produces an amplitude vector whose marked probability is $1$.

results.title: Read covering a base of a circular genome
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A read of length `L` starting at position `s` of a circular genome of length `G` covers base `x` when `x` is one of `s, s + 1, …, s + L - 1 (mod G)`, i.e. `(x - s) mod G < L`.

results.title: Depth of coverage of a base
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The depth of coverage of base `x`: the number of reads covering it.

results.title: Normalized count of read start tuples
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The totalized normalized count `|E| / G ^ N` of a set of start tuples. For `0 < G`, this is the probability when the `N` start positions are independent and uniform on `Fin G`. If `G = 0` and `N > 0`, the sample space is empty and this value is zero, so it is not a probability law. For `N = 0`, there is one empty start tuple, even when `G = 0`.

results.title: Normalized count agrees with the totalized uniform measure
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `normalizedCount` agrees with Mathlib's totalized uniform measure on all start tuples. This measure is a probability law only when the sample space is nonempty.

results.title: Exact coverage count
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `L ≤ G`, base `x` is uncovered by all `N` reads for exactly `(G - L) ^ N` of the `G ^ N` start tuples.

results.title: Exact depth law (count form)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `L ≤ G`, base `x` is covered by exactly `k` reads for `N.choose k * L ^ k * (G - L) ^ (N - k)` of the start tuples.

results.title: Exact uncovered probability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Exact uncovered probability (Clarke–Carbon, Lander–Waterman, circular genome): `(1 - L / G) ^ N` for `L ≤ G`.

results.title: Exact depth law
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The depth at a fixed base is binomial with `N` trials and success probability `L / G`, for `L ≤ G`.

results.title: Lander–Waterman limit for the uncovered fraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With read length `L` fixed, genome lengths `G N ≥ L`, and coverage `N L / G_N → c` as the number of reads `N → ∞`, the probability that a given base is uncovered tends to `e^{-c}`.

results.title: The coverage depth tends to Poisson(`c`)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Under the hypotheses of `tendsto_normalizedCount_uncovered`, the probability that a given base is covered by exactly `k` reads tends to `e^{-c} c^k / k.factorial`.

results.title: Read with no successor
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Read `j` has no successor when no other read starts in the `L - 1` positions after it, `starts j + 1, …, starts j + L - 1 (mod G)` (reads starting at the same position are not successors of each other). In Lander and Waterman's terms such a read is counted as ending an island, but several no-successor reads can lie in one island, so this is not the island count.

results.title: Count of no-successor reads (exact)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `L ≤ G`, summed over the reads, the number of start tuples in which read `j` has no successor is `N * G * (G - (L - 1)) ^ (N - 1)`. This counts no-successor reads, not island ends: a start tuple can have several no-successor reads in one island.

results.title: Expected number of no-successor reads (exact)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `0 < G` and `L ≤ G`, the expected number of reads with no successor is `N (1 - (L - 1) / G) ^ (N - 1)`. The `0 < G` hypothesis is essential: at `G = 0` and `N > 0`, the right-hand expression is `N` while the sum of totalized normalized counts is zero.

used_by: Pulley principle, LogDet distances and Felsenstein zone

results.title: Min-plus cost semiring
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: The cost semiring: `MinTropical (WithTop ℕ)`, with `min` as addition and `+` as multiplication.

results.title: Total substitution cost of a labeling
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The total substitution cost of a labeling `x` of the non-root vertices of `t` with root state `s`: the sum over all edges of the cost `untrop (P a b)` from the parent's state `a` to the child's state `b`.

results.title: Labeling agrees with the observed leaf states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The labeling `x` (with root state `s`) agrees with the observed states `σ` at every leaf.

results.title: Tropical leaf weights of observed states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The leaf weights of the observed states `σ`: the tropical one (cost `0`) at the observed state and the tropical zero (cost `⊤`) at every other state.

results.title: Tropical weight of a labeling equals its edge cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The weight of a labeling in the tropical semiring is its edge cost if it agrees with the leaf states and `⊤` otherwise.

results.title: Sankoff's algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The minimum cost of the subtree `t` given the state `s` at its root, computed by Felsenstein's pruning recursion over the tropical semiring.

results.title: Sankoff's algorithm computes the small-parsimony cost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `sankoff σ t s` is the minimum total edge cost over all labelings of the non-root vertices that agree with the observed states at the leaves (with root state `s`).

results.title: Sankoff's cost is a lower bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Sankoff's cost is a lower bound for the cost of every labeling that agrees with the leaf states.

results.title: Sankoff's cost is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Sankoff's cost is attained: if it is finite, some labeling that agrees with the leaf states has exactly this cost. (It is `⊤` exactly when every agreeing labeling uses a forbidden change, or when `t` is a single leaf whose observed state is not `s`.)

results.title: Sankoff's recursion at a leaf
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Sankoff's recursion at a leaf: cost `0` at the observed state, `⊤` elsewhere.

results.title: Sankoff's recursion at an internal vertex
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Sankoff's recursion at an internal vertex: the cost of state `s` is the sum, over the two children, of the minimum over the child's state `a` of the edge cost from `s` to `a` plus the child's cost at `a`.

results.title: Unit substitution cost
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The unit cost: `0` for no change and `1` for a change of state.

results.title: Tree with unit costs on every edge
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Every edge of the tree carries the unit cost.

results.title: Fitch's algorithm
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The set of candidate states at the root of the subtree and the number of changes counted so far. The edge weights of the tree are ignored. Each child is evaluated once per node, so the recursion makes one call per vertex.

results.title: Fitch's algorithm computes the small-parsimony score
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On a binary tree with unit costs, Fitch's count equals the minimum, over root states, of Sankoff's cost.

results.title: Fitch's root set is the set of optimal root states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On a binary tree with unit costs, a root state is in Fitch's set if and only if Sankoff's cost at that state is the minimum.
